etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old French proverbe, from Latin proverbium.

definitions.definition: A commonly used sentence expressing popular wisdom.
(obsolete) A striking or paradoxical assertion; an obscure saying; an enigma; a parable.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, John 16:29:
quote.text: His disciples said unto him, Lo, now speakest thou plainly, and speakest no proverb.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A familiar illustration; a subject of contemptuous reference.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Deuteronomy 28:37:
quote.text: Thou shalt become an astonishment, a proverb, and a by word, among all nations.

definitions.definition: To name in, or as, a proverb.

quote.text: Am I not sung and proverbed for a fool / In every street, do they not say, "How well / Are come upon him his deserts?"

quote.citation: c. 1591–1595 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Romeo and Ivliet”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iv]:
quote.text: I am proverbed with a grandsire phrase.
